Rose Bowl Parade. Also known as the Tournament of Roses Parade, an elaborate New Year's Day celebration held annually in Pasadena, California, featuring floats decorated entirely with fresh flowers and greenery. The parade has been held every January first since eighteen ninety and is one of the most prestigious parades in the United States. The event originated from the Pasadena Valley Hunt Club's winter festival and has evolved into a globally televised spectacle drawing millions of viewers.

The parade is held every January first in Pasadena, California, except when January first falls on a Sunday, when it is moved to January second. The parade features elaborate floats created by civic organizations, community groups, and corporations, entirely covered with fresh flowers—no artificial flowers are allowed. The parade tradition began in eighteen ninety as a way to celebrate Southern California's winter bloom and demonstrate the mild climate to attract settlers and tourists.

The Rose Bowl football game, traditionally played on New Year's Day featuring the top-ranked teams from the Pac-Twelve and Big Ten conferences, follows the parade. A notable celebrity or public figure, called the Grand Marshal, rides in the leading float, with past marshals including presidents, athletes, and entertainment icons. The parade route spans five and a half miles through Pasadena streets, attracting crowds along the entire path with millions more watching via television broadcast. Floats typically feature themes celebrating achievements, dreams, innovation, or regional culture, with marching bands, equestrian units, and walking groups accompanying the floats.
